outcome: Redington gives research teams a recorded environment for every experiment and a supported path from a trained model to a served endpoint.
overview: Research groups reach a point where models are trained on whatever hardware someone could book, and nothing about the result is reproducible — not the environment, not the data version, not the serving path. Red Hat OpenShift AI puts model development, training and serving on the same container platform the rest of the estate already runs, so an experiment has a recorded environment and a trained model has a deployment route that is not a laptop. The gain is reproducibility and shared access to scarce accelerators. Redington scopes it against named research workloads and measures time from experiment to a served model.

benefits.text: Experiments carry a recorded environment, so a result can be reproduced months later
benefits.limits: Reproducibility also needs data versioning, which is a separate discipline the platform enables but does not impose

benefits.text: Scarce accelerators are shared through scheduling rather than booked by whoever asked first
benefits.limits: Sharing depends on an agreed allocation policy; without one, scheduling makes contention visible rather than fair

benefits.text: A trained model has a supported serving path instead of being re-implemented for production
benefits.limits: Serving readiness still requires the model to meet latency and evaluation criteria the platform does not set

residency: Runs on customer-controlled infrastructure, so research data and trained model weights stay inside the institution’s own boundary

notFor.situation: A group whose work is entirely on a managed cloud ML service already
notFor.why: The platform’s value is a controlled environment you operate; that is a cost, not a benefit, if a managed service already fits

notFor.situation: A single researcher with a single workstation
notFor.why: Platform overhead exceeds any sharing or reproducibility gain at that scale

scope:
Model: Redington solutions engineering with an accredited Red Hat implementation partner · Duration: 10–14 weeks to a first research workload in production, hardware lead time excluded
Support model: Vendor subscription support for the platform; Redington coordinates the vendor case and the accelerator vendor case where hardware is in scope.
1) Assessment — candidate workloads, data readiness, accelerator sizing and facility constraints
2) Design — cluster and accelerator topology, allocation policy, registry and serving path
3) Build — platform, accelerator enablement, workbenches, registry and serving
4) Onboard and hand over — first workload trained and served on the platform, runbooks handed over
deliverables: A training run can be repeated from the registry record and produces a comparable result
Two research groups draw from the same accelerator pool under the agreed allocation policy
A registered model is promoted to a served endpoint without being re-implemented
